title: Comparator Interface: Custom Sorting & Lambda Chains
summary: Write reusable external sorting strategies with Comparator<T>: anonymous classes, lambda expressions, Comparator.comparing(), and thenComparing().
learningObjectives: Master java.util.Comparator<T> to establish external, decoupled sorting strategies
Compose clean, declarative multi-level comparator chains with Comparator.comparing() and thenComparing()
Invert sort order dynamically using comparator.reversed()
Safely handle null elements in sort pipelines using Comparator.nullsFirst() and nullsLast()
expectedOutcomes: Ability to architect flexible, customizable sorting engines for e-commerce, banking, and analytics
Mastery of modern functional comparator composition in Java 8+

activities.title: Practical Context: Flight Booking Engine Search Filters

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Flight Booking Engine Search Filters
analogy.story:
When you search for airline flights online, an airline ticket does not possess a single 'natural' way to be displayed. A student traveler wants flights sorted by 'Cheapest Price First'. A business executive wants 'Shortest Flight Duration First'. A morning commuter wants 'Earliest Departure Time First'.

The Flight class itself remains completely unchanged. Instead, the booking engine applies external lenses (Comparators) to sort the exact same list of flights according to whichever criteria the user selected in the dropdown menu.

The `Comparator` interface represents this exact external lens: decoupling the sorting policy from the data model.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Comparator defines external sorting strategies that can be swapped dynamically at runtime without modifying the underlying class definition.

activities.title: Modern Comparator Architecture: Composition, Inversion & Null-Safety

keyTakeaways: Comparator<T> is a @FunctionalInterface whose single abstract method is int compare(T o1, T o2)
Comparator.comparing(Function) creates type-safe comparators using method references
thenComparing(Function) chains secondary and tertiary tie-breakers
reversed() inverts the sorting order cleanly
Comparator.nullsFirst() and nullsLast() protect against NullPointerExceptions in dirty data streams

activities.title: Null-Safe Multi-Tier User Profile Sorter
activities.description: Trace a dirty user database records sorter that handles null departments and null names gracefully.

steps.description: Comparator.nullsLast(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER) wraps the string comparator, guaranteeing null departments are pushed to the end without crashing.
thenComparing(Profile::getUsername) breaks ties within the same department.
profiles.sort(comp) sorts in-place using Java's list.sort() default method.

questions.question: What is the result of invoking 'Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge).reversed()' on a list of Person objects?
options: It sorts by age descending (oldest person first)
It reverses the entire list without comparing
questions.explanation: Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge) sorts in natural ascending order. Calling .reversed() inverts the comparator's comparison results, sorting ages in descending order.

questions.question: How do you prevent a NullPointerException when comparing a field that can be null using Comparator.comparing()?
options: Surround the comparator in a try-catch block
Use the two-argument overload: Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor, Comparator.nullsLast(...))
questions.explanation: Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator) accepts a custom key comparator. Supplying Comparator.nullsFirst(...) or nullsLast(...) safely handles null key values without throwing NullPointerException.

activities.title: Senior Engineer Interview: Performance of Lambda Comparators

qaList.question: Does using 'Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary)' cause autoboxing overhead compared to writing a raw lambda?
qaList.answer: No. When using primitive specialized methods like 'comparingDouble()', 'comparingInt()', or 'comparingLong()', the extractor function is a ToDoubleFunction, ToIntFunction, or ToLongFunction which extracts unboxed primitive values directly and compares them using Double.compare() or Integer.compare(). If you accidentally used the generic 'Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary)' where getSalary() returns double, Java would autobox the double into a java.lang.Double object on every comparison, generating millions of transient heap objects during large sorts. Always use the primitive-specialized comparingInt/Long/Double overloads for primitive properties.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I know how to write declarative comparators with Comparator.comparing() and thenComparing()
I understand how to invert sort order with .reversed()
I know how to handle null elements and null keys safely with nullsFirst and nullsLast
I know to use primitive specialized comparators (comparingInt, comparingDouble) to avoid autoboxing

practiceProblems.title: Flight Booking Sorter Pipeline
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method sortFlights(List<Flight> flights) that sorts flights primarily by price ascending, tie-breaking by durationMinutes ascending using Comparator.comparing().

practiceProblems.title: String Sorter: Length Ascending, Lexical Tie-Break
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method sortWords(List<String> words) that sorts strings by length ascending, tie-breaking alphabetically in-place.

practiceProblems.title: Null-Safe Descending String Sorter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method sortWithNullsLast(List<String> words) that sorts strings descending alphabetically, placing null strings at the very end of the list.

practiceProblems.title: Reverse Arbitrary Comparator Utility
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a generic static method <T> Comparator<T> invert(Comparator<T> comp) that returns an inverted version of the supplied comparator without modifying the original.

practiceProblems.title: Sort by Frequency Then Value
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method sortByFrequency(List<Integer> nums) that sorts integers primarily by their occurrence frequency descending, and tie-breaks by numerical value ascending.
